title: Readiness Criteria to Move On to Lesson 2 — Memorize A and D Chords and Master Chord Changes
summary: In this brief guidance, JustinGuitar outlines concrete criteria to decide when a beginner is ready to advance from Lesson 1 to Lesson 2. The core requirements are: memorize the A and D chords so you can form and identify them by feel without looking at a chart, and be able to change between those two chords at a steady pace (starting around 30 changes per minute, with a long-term goal of about 60 changes per minute). He emphasizes a practical timeline (most students can reach readiness in 2–4 weeks, with a hard cap of about 4 weeks). If progress stalls or boredom appears after a couple of weeks, it’s acceptable to move on to the next lesson to keep practice engaging, especially if you’ve also managed to play a song and maintain chord-change practice. He also notes that if in doubt, you can watch the final left-handed Lesson 1 video for reassurance before proceeding, and he signs off when readiness is confirmed.

summary: In this beginner-focused micro-lesson, the instructor explains how to strum only the appropriate strings for common open chords, emphasizing that new players should aim to avoid the thickest strings on D and A chords while recognizing that early-stage mistakes are normal. title: Guitar TAB Basics: Six-String Layout, Frets, Chords, and Rhythm Essentials
summary: JustinGuitar’s beginner-focused tutorial introduces guitar tablature (TAB) as a practical alternative to traditional notation for guitarists. The video explains that TAB uses six horizontal lines representing the six strings, with the bottom line corresponding to the thickest (low E) string and the top line to the thinnest (high E). Numbers on the lines indicate frets to press, while a zero means the string is played open. The presenter demonstrates a C-like idea of fretting across the six strings by showing an E major-like layout (0-2-2-1-0-0) and explains that notes can be played on multiple strings, so rhythm in TAB is not shown by default. He also notes that fingering isn’t specified by TAB—the learner must apply logic or follow guidance—emphasizing that early TAB literacy is a valuable skill. The video concludes by contrasting TAB’s lack of rhythm notation with the importance of listening to a riff or song for rhythm and by recommending that beginners begin reading TAB as soon as possible.
